messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Callum Delaney is a 35-year-old single man of Irish descent who works as a special education teacher at a public middle school in a mid-sized Midwestern city. He presented for an initial intake following a street robbery that occurred approximately eight months ago, and his PCL-5 score of 58 places him well within the severe range of post-traumatic stress. He described the incident with a precision that was itself striking: walking home alone at dusk after a late parent-teacher conference, he was approached from behind by two men who shoved him hard against a chain-link fence, one pressing a forearm across the back of his neck while the other demanded his wallet and phone. He remembered the specific pressure on his cervical spine, the metallic smell of the fence, the sound of one man shouting inches from his ear. He did not fight back. A patrol car passed slowly at the far end of the block and kept moving. Within minutes it was over, but for Callum, it has not been over since.

In the weeks following the robbery, Callum found that certain experiences reached back into that evening and pulled it forward with a vividness he described as photographic — not like remembering, but like being shown. The sound of shouting, whether a colleague raising his voice across the school hallway or a student having a meltdown in class, could snap him instantly back to that alley, the scene assembling itself image by image with the same cold clarity. The dull ache that had settled into his neck since the assault functioned in the same way: on difficult days in the classroom, when tension accumulated in his shoulders and crept upward, the somatic reminder was enough to flood him with the full sensory record of the attack. Even the sight of a police officer — a presence that might reasonably signal safety — had become a trigger rather than a comfort, because the patrol car that passed without stopping had lodged itself as proof that no one was coming. Each of these cues reliably returned him to the memory, and the memory, when it arrived, brought with it not only fear but a fierce, disorienting rage, followed almost immediately by guilt at feeling that rage at all.

That guilt had become one of the most corrosive features of his presentation. Callum had come to believe, with a certainty he could not argue himself out of, that someone else — someone more alert, more capable, more fundamentally adequate — would simply not have been in this situation. He had stayed late at school. He had walked that route. He had frozen. These appraisals of personal inadequacy were not abstract; they pressed directly on his sense of ongoing threat, convincing him that he remained vulnerable precisely because of some deficiency in himself, and that the world required constant vigilance as a result. He found himself unable to relax even in demonstrably safe settings — in his own apartment, in the school staffroom — because the belief that he was inadequate to protect himself made safety feel like an illusion. He had begun scanning for exits the moment he entered any room, a habit so automatic now that he clocked the fire doors in his own classroom before his students arrived each morning.

The hypervigilance fed back relentlessly into the memories it was meant to prevent. The more he monitored his environment for threat, the more his nervous system remained primed, and the more readily the photographic recall returned — the fence, the neck, the shouting, the passing car. Each intrusion confirmed the appraisals that had generated the vigilance in the first place: he was inadequate, he was not safe, he had to stay alert. The loop had tightened over months. He had quietly stopped attending the after-school staff gatherings where voices sometimes rose in laughter or argument, and a colleague he had considered a close friend had stopped reaching out after several unanswered invitations.

What finally brought Callum in was a moment in his classroom when a student knocked over a chair with a loud bang and Callum, in front of twenty-two children, dropped into a crouch behind his desk. He described the shame of it with a flat, exhausted voice. He was not sure what he hoped for, only that he could not keep living inside a body that treated every school day as a continuation of that night.
